Au-delà d’Amira Elghawaby : qu’en disent: Beyond Amira Elghawaby: What Do Women Affected by Islamophobia in Quebec Have to Say?
« Il faut en parler, il faut toujours en: “We have to talk about it, we always have to talk about it”
Safa Chebbi, Nafija Rahman et Idil Issa: Safa Chebbi, Nafija Rahman and Idil Issa Photo: Ahmed El Moudden
La nomination d’Amira Elghawaby en tant: The appointment of Amira Elghawaby as Canada’s Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia drew a wave of reactions and criticism from politicians and the media. Some of her past statements were dug up, and her credibility was repeatedly called into question. Despite her apology, <l1>the National Assembly unanimously called for her resignation, with some even demanding that her position be abolished</l1>.
Dans le cadre de la Semaine de sensibili: Coming during Islamophobia Awareness Week in Quebec, which commemorates the 2017 attack on the Grand Mosque of Quebec City, the controversy was painful for many Muslims. Although some members of the community spoke out on social media, they had no chance to express themselves in a discussion setting. To fill that gap, La Converse invited racialized Muslim women from different backgrounds to start a dialogue on the subject in a caring and safe environment.
<strong>« Il faut en parler, il faut tou: “We have to talk about it, we always have to talk about it”
Les douces lueurs de la librairie Maktab: The soft glow of the Maktaba bookstore welcomes Idil Issa, Safa Chebbi and Nafija Rahman on a Friday evening. As the owner, Sundus, greets us with hot tea, she asks us to take off our shoes before sitting down in the Majlis. “[The Majlis is] traditionally the place where community members gather to discuss events and local issues, exchange news, receive guests and socialize,” she explains. In this intimate, warm atmosphere, our guests open up to us.
Idil, étudiante en droit, fondatrice de: Idil, a law student, founder of Muslim Women Against Racism and cofounder of Mouvement Montréal, opens the discussion by explaining why it is important to have this kind of conversation. “First of all, I’ve known Amira for a long time, she’s a close friend. What’s happening to her is not only important in itself; it’s also the questions about Islamophobia that it raises that affect me personally, and professionally too.”
Les propos d’Idil font écho à ceux de Sa: Idil’s words echo those of Safa, who doesn’t know Amira but also feels the repercussions of this controversy. “Amira represents me in a way. Every time a woman with an Arabic or Muslim name gets media attention, I feel concerned,” says Safa, a decolonial anti-racist activist and master’s student in sociology. She also expresses her dismay at a sense of déjà vu in the exclusion, adding that “she finds it disheartening that we’re doing the same thing again… <l1>We saw it with the appointment of Bochra Manaï</l1> and we’re living it again, but it was predictable.” When Bochra Manaï was appointed to the Office of the Commissioner for the Fight Against Racism and Systemic Discrimination, the Legault government judged that “<l2>it was a mistake on the city’s part</l2>” because Ms. Manaï, like Ms. Elghawaby, is an active opponent of Bill 21.
Nafija, une organisatrice communautaire: Nafija, a committed community organizer, finds herself caught up in the fallout of this controversy in spite of herself. Candidly, she admits that “it came out of nowhere.” Exasperated, she continues: “I said to myself, ‘Oh no!’ Here we go again with this chapter! We have to say why, why we have to exist, and why our existence is valid.” She shares her fears for her safety, having lived through traumatic experiences during similar controversies. “I’ve already been attacked several times in the street, and now I’m wondering: is all of that going to start again? Do I have to go through that again?” Still, she is determined to break the silence. With a surge of hope, she insists: “We have to talk about it, always talk about it. We’re going to do this in a safe space and we’re going to talk about it.”
Repensant à la vive réaction des médias: Looking back on the media’s strong reaction and the political uproar caused by Ms. Elghawaby’s appointment, Idil expresses her pain: “It was a difficult moment for me, I was shocked. You can disagree with what Amira said, but these attacks went beyond all measure.” Safa points out that “even though Amira apologized, it didn’t change anything.” Nafija adds that it wasn’t enough to calm the anger of the political class, which seemed to want to humiliate her. “You have to make yourself small, you have to bend. I had the image of public punishment, of a witch hunt [like in medieval times],” she tells us.
Idil approfondit les considérations de s: Idil builds on her fellow guests’ points by stressing that Muslim women are constantly dehumanized. “Muslim women aren’t allowed to have made mistakes, to be human. Quebec politicians have made statements that deserved a call for their resignation, but they’re still in their positions,” Idil says indignantly. She is referring to <l1>the erroneous remarks about immigration made by Minister Jean Boulet during the last election campaign.</l1> The government’s official response was to remove the Immigration portfolio from Mr. Boulet, though it should be noted that he remained at the head of the Ministry of Labour.
Ancienne candidate aux élections municip: A former municipal election candidate, Idil believes Muslim women experience a great deal of political violence. “Muslim women are instrumentalized for political gain,” she says. Along the same lines, Safa states: “Racism still pays politically: the more racist things you say, the more votes you win.” She is categorical: “Criticizing Quebec is a right and a duty in a democracy.” With a determined look, she says, “What Amira said is a criticism that could have been made by a white person; but if a white person had said those things, they wouldn’t have been received the same way. There’s a double standard.” Nafija and Idil listen closely, nodding as Safa continues: “Even if she hadn’t said those things, the problem lies in who she is, not in what she says,” she argues. Safa adds: <l1>“This position [Canada’s Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia] is being called into question anyway.</l1> We have to get back to the root of the problem: the denial of Islamophobia in Quebec. For me, Amira isn’t the problem; this controversy is just the tip of the Islamophobia iceberg.”
Nafija, le cœur lourd, exprime son indig: Nafija, with a heavy heart, expresses her indignation at the way Quebec’s French-language press presented Amira’s appointment, her statements and Ms. Elghawaby herself. “We always see her with a tense expression, [as if she were mean], the villain. We never see her smile, they describe her as an activist. All of this reminds me of the comments I often get. ‘You don’t have Quebec values, you don’t understand Quebec, you don’t belong here, especially in a high-level position. How dare you?’”
Idil admet que, si elle s’était contenté: Idil admits that if she had relied on the media alone, she would have been angry, because the story was presented in a sensationalist way. She explains: “If I had been born here, if I had been raised here and I only read the headlines without digging deeper, I’d be angry. [The media] presented it in the worst possible way: it was deliberate, to provoke that kind of reaction,” the young woman believes. She is not satisfied with how the rest of Canada handled the affair either. “It’s very easy and far too simplistic to point fingers and claim it’s Quebec’s problem.” She recalls the murder of <l1>the Afzaal family in Ontario</l1>. Safa agrees, adding that “racism and Islamophobia aren’t limited to this geographic area; it’s a whole system.”
Nafija, qui s’identifie à Amira Elghawab: Nafija, who identifies with Amira Elghawaby, notes that one of the recurring criticisms aimed at racialized people who enter the public sphere is “their ‘foreign’ origin, no matter how long they’ve been here or how they identify.” For her, who has only ever known Quebec, shaping her sense of identity wasn’t easy. “Before, I refused to be Québécoise, because it was refused to me. I only know Montréal, only Quebec. I don’t know Bangladesh. I grew up here,” she says.
La vie de Nafija a été profondément pert: Nafija’s life was deeply disrupted when she chose to openly embrace her identity. “The moment I started wearing the hijab, I suddenly wasn’t the same person anymore. The way others looked at me changed, and so did their attitude. I was no longer the same person in the eyes of my community,” she confides bitterly. “I grew up in a Quebec community that calls itself feminist, but that same community said my choices were the wrong ones and that I needed to think differently. I couldn’t consider myself a feminist, or even a Quebecer, because those aren’t values that are ‘ours,’ and it follows me all the time,” she says.
C’est d’ailleurs cette différence qui fa: It is precisely this difference that means the three women don’t see themselves in the National Assembly’s demands, made on behalf of Quebec, that Ms. Elghawaby apologize and resign. “Who is this Quebec that doesn’t agree with what Amira said or doesn’t accept her apology?” asks Nafija. “Either they think we all agree, or they think some people don’t count in this Quebec, because nobody asked me, and yet I’m part of it.”
Safa se joint à Nafija lorsque cette der: Safa joins Nafija when the latter voices her disagreement with the conventional definition of Quebec. “I identify more with Montréal. As soon as I leave Montréal, the way people look at me changes,” she explains. Safa remembers Tunisia, which she left in the midst of a dictatorship, when the hijab was banned. “Here, honestly, in a country that prides itself on being a democracy and has a fairly long democratic history, I find myself facing the same thing [with Bill 21],” she says, sounding disappointed.
Idil, pour sa part, dit avoir « adopté l: Idil, for her part, says she “adopted Quebec, but in terms of belonging, it’s hard to feel that I’m part of Quebec.” She acknowledges that Muslim Quebecers “have been through many ordeals: Bill 62, the Charter of Rights and the Charter of Values, the Quebec City attack, Bill 21 and now this [the Elghawaby affair].” Having lived in several Canadian provinces where the Somali community is larger, Idil says she feels more Canadian. As a Black Muslim woman, she believes that doesn’t stop her from identifying as Canadian. “Recently, I decided that I didn’t want to be identified as Somali-Canadian. I want to be seen as Canadian. If a white woman can say she’s Canadian, then so can I!”
<strong>« La machine est lancée ; mainte: “The machine is in motion; now we have to keep going”
Alors que la nuit s’installe sur le Vieu: As night settles over Old Montréal, the conversation, livelier than ever, takes on notes of hope, with the women discussing possible solutions to bring about change in the way some politicians treat Muslim Quebecers.
L’étudiante en droit estime que les gouv: The law student believes that the provincial and federal governments are instrumentalizing Quebec’s history. She points out that “Quebec claims the primacy of individual rights, but tramples the right of visibly Muslim women to work.” She states: “Law is power.” She expresses her despair at the National Assembly and says: “If the 2017 shooting at the Grand Mosque of Quebec City didn’t make politicians understand that there’s a real problem of Islamophobia, I don’t know what will convince them. Islamophobia doesn’t exist, and yet it kills.”
Selon elle, la solution serait de s’enga: In her view, the solution is to get involved in the public and political sphere, saying that “we have to take action, we have to use democratic tools, run in elections again. Civil society has to be stronger.” Although Safa expects nothing from the politicians currently in office, she insists on the importance of “reminding people of democratic values, with justice and equality as our compass.”
Nafija, quant à elle, appelle à la respo: Nafija, for her part, calls on politicians to be accountable: “We are the Quebec people, the Canadian people. We elected them, they are accountable to all communities. With great power comes great responsibility.” She encourages her fellow citizens not to give up the fight: “It’s always a struggle – the machine is in motion; now we have to keep going.”
La ville autour de nous commence à s’ani: The city around us is starting to come alive, and the tea is now cold. We put our shoes back on and get ready to leave the Maktaba bookstore. Idil, Safa and Nafija thank us for the opportunity to share their stories. Sundus, the owner, wishes us a good evening and reminds us that everyone is always welcome in the Majlis.
